    #Part (b)

    #Part (i)

    Let x1​=θ.

    Let x2​=θ˙.

    Derivatives of state variables,

    x˙1​=θ˙=x2​

    x˙2​=θ¨

    Substituting into differential equation,

    0=x˙2​−(k1​−x1​2)x2​+k2​x1​

    x˙2​=−k2​x1​+(k1​−x1​2)x2​

    Expressing in state-space form,

    {x˙1​x˙2​​}=[0−k2​​1k1​−x1​2​]{x1​x2​​}

    #Part (ii)

    State-space equations,

    f1​=x˙1​=x2​

    f2​=x˙2​=−k2​x1​+k1​x2​−x1​2x2​

    Derivatives of equations,

    f11′​=∂x1​∂f1​​=0

    f12′​=∂x2​∂f1​​=1

    f21′​=∂x1​∂f2​​=−k2​−2x1​x2​

    f22′​=∂x2​∂f2​​=k1​−x1​2

    Jacobian matrix,

    A=∂X∂F​​(0,0)​=[f11′​f21′​​f12′​f22′​​](0,0)​

    A=[0−k2​−2x1​x2​​1k1​−x1​2​](0,0)​

    A=[0−k2​​1k1​​]

    Expressing in state-space form,

    {x˙1​x˙2​​}=[0−k2​​1k1​​]{x1​x2​​}

    #Part (iii)

    Determinant of matrix,

    0=det​A−λI​​

    0=det​−λ−k2​​1k1​−λ​​

    0=−λ(k1​−λ)−(−k2​)

    0=λ2−k1​λ+k2​

    Roots of characteristic equation,

    λ1,2​=2a−b±b2−4ac​​

    λ1,2​=2k1​±k1​2−4k2​​​

    λ1,2​=2k1​​±4k1​2​−k2​​

    For the system to be stable, the roots has to lie
    to the left of the imaginary axis of the pole plot.

    Range of values,

    k1​<0

    Overdamped,

    4k1​2​−k2​>0

    k1​2>4k2​

    k1​>2k2​​

    Underdamped,

    4k1​2​−k2​<0

    k1​2<4k2​

    k1​<2k2​​

    Critically damped,

    4k1​2​−k2​=0

    k1​2=4k2​

    k1​=2k2​​

    #Question 4

    #Part (a)

    Assumptions:

    • Side force equation Δv˙=… is neglected
    • Negligible roll rate Δp≈0
    • Ixx​Ixz​​≈0 and Izz​Ixz​​≈0

    Simplifying the rolling moment equation,

    Δp˙​−(Ixx​Ixz​​)Δr˙=Lv​Δv+Lp​Δp+Lr​Δr+Lδr​​Δδr​+Lδa​​Δδa​

    0=Lv​Δv+Lr​Δr

    Δv=−Lv​Lr​​Δr

    Δβ=−Lβ​Lr​​Δr

    Simplifying the yawing moment equation,

    Δr˙−(Izz​Ixz​​)Δp˙​=Nv​Δv+Np​Δp+Nr​Δr+Nδr​​Δδr​+Nδa​​Δδa​

    Δr˙=Nv​Δv+Nr​Δr

    Δr˙=Nβ​Δβ+Nr​Δr

    Δr˙=Nβ​(−Lβ​Lr​​Δr)+Nr​Δr

    0=Δr˙−(−Lβ​Nβ​Lr​​+Nr​)Δr

    0=Δr˙−(Lβ​−Nβ​Lr​+Nr​Lβ​​)Δr

    0=Δr˙+Lβ​Lβ​Nr​−Lr​Nβ​​Δr

    Characteristic equation,

    0=λ+Lβ​Lβ​Nr​−Lr​Nβ​​

    λ=Lβ​Lr​Nβ​−Lβ​Nr​​

    For a stable spiral mode, eigenvalue λ<0,

    0>Lβ​Lr​Nβ​−Lβ​Nr​​

    0>Lr​Nβ​−Lβ​Nr​

    Lβ​Nr​>Lr​Nβ​

    Pure yawing motion equation,

    Δψ¨​+1.72Δψ˙​+4.537Δψ=−2.21Δδr​

    −Δβ¨​−1.72Δβ˙​−4.537Δβ=−2.21Δδr​

    Δβ¨​+1.72Δβ˙​+4.537Δβ=2.21Δδr​

    Equation is a 2nd-order non-homogeneous DE.

    #Part (i)

    Characteristic equation,

    0=aλ2+bλ+c

    0=λ2+1.72λ+4.537

    0=s2+(2ζωn​)s+ωn​2

    Natural frequency of motion,

    ωn​=4.537​=2.13 rad/s

    Damping ratio of motion,

    ζ=2(2.13)1.72​=0.40375

    #Part (ii)

    Substituting step rudder input Δδr​=10,

    Δβ¨​+1.72Δβ˙​+4.537Δβ=2.21(10)

    Δβ¨​+1.72Δβ˙​+4.537Δβ=22.1

    Performing Laplace transform,

    s2Δβ(s)+1.72sΔβ(s)+4.537Δβ(s)=s22.1​

    (s2+1.72s+4.537)Δβ(s)=s22.1​

    Δβ(s)=s(s2+1.72s+4.537)22.1​

    Δβ(s)=sA​+s2+1.72s+4.537Bs+C​

    Partial fractions

    Solving the partial fractions,

    22.1=A(s2+1.72s+4.537)+Bs2+Cs

    22.1=(A+B)s2+(1.72A+C)s+4.537A

    Let s=0.

    22.1=4.537A

    A=4.8711

    Let s=1.

    22.1=A+B+1.72A+C+4.537A

    22.1=7.257A+B+C

    22.1=7.257(4.8711)+B+C

    B=−13.250−C (1)

    Let s=2.

    22.1=4A+4B+3.44A+2C+4.537A

    22.1=11.977A+4B+2C

    22.1=11.977(4.8711)+4(−13.250−C)+2C

    22.1=5.3412−2C

    C=−8.3794

    B=−4.871

    Expression for sideslip response,

    Δβ(s)=s4.8711​−s2+1.72s+4.5374.871s+8.3794​

    Δβ(s)=s4.8711​−4.871(s2+1.72s+4.537s+1.72​)

    Inverse Laplace transforms to use,

    L{eatcos(bt)}=(s−a)2+b2s−a​

    L{eatsin(bt)}=(s−a)2+b2b​

    Rewriting the 2nd term,

    s2+1.72s+4.537s+1.72​

    =(s+0.86)2+3.7974s+0.86​+(s+0.86)2+3.79740.86​

    =(s+0.86)2+1.94892s+0.86​+1.94890.86​⋅(s+0.86)2+1.948921.9489​

    Inverse Laplace transform of 2nd term,

    L{s2+1.72s+4.537s+1.72​}−1

    =e−0.86tcos(1.9489t)+1.94890.86​e−0.86tsin(1.9489t)

    =e−0.86tcos(1.9489t)+0.44127e−0.86tsin(1.9489t)

    =e−0.86t(cos1.9489t+0.44127sin1.9489t)

    Expression for sideslip response,

    Δβ(t)=4.8711−4.871e−0.86t(cos1.9489t+0.44127sin1.9489t)

    #Part (d)

    Static margin is given by,

    SM=cˉxNP​−xCG​​

    Maneuver margin is given by,

    MM=cˉxNP​−xCG​​+2μηH​VH​CLαt​​​​

    where μ is the relative density parameter

    Since maneuver margin is greater than static margin, longitudinal static stability increases as neutral point of the aircraft during a maneuver shifts aftwards due
    to the additional lift generated during a pull-up maneuver.

    #Question 2

    #Part (a)

    Sweptback wing:

    • Aircraft experiences positive sideslip (to the right)
    • Right wing has a larger normal velocity component
    • Right wing generates more lift and thus more drag
    • Drag asymmetry causes a positive yaw moment (to the right)
    • Aircraft returns to its original orientation (stabilizing effect)

    Dihedral wing:

    • Aircraft experiences positive sideslip (to the right)
    • Right wing has a positive normal sideslip velocity component
    • Left wing has a negative normal sideslip velocity component
    • Right wing has a higher angle of attack than the left wing
    • Right wing generates more lift and thus more drag
    • Drag asymmetry causes a positive yaw moment (to the right)
    • Aircraft returns to its original orientation (stabilizing effect)

    High wing:

    • Aircraft experiences positive sideslip (to the right)
    • Right wing has a higher angle of attack due to sideslip
    • Right wing generates more lift and thus more drag
    • Drag asymmetry causes a positive yaw moment (to the right)
    • Aircraft returns to its original orientation (stabilizing effect)

    #Part (c)

    Destabilizing yawing moment:

    • Positive rolling motion — aircraft is banking to the right
    • Positive aileron deflection — right aileron down, left aileron up
    • Right wing generates more lift and thus more drag
    • Drag asymmetry causes positive yawing moment (to the right)
    • Aircraft yaws in the direction of the spin, aggravating the spin

    #Part (c)

    • Propeller generates a normal force NP​ when it is at an angle of attack
    • Thrust of the propeller tends to create stabilizing moment (pitch down)
    • Normal force NP​ tends to create a destabilizing moment (pitch up)
    • As angle of attack increases, NP​ increases, higher pitch-up moment
    • Pitch-up moment becomes greater than the pitch-down moment
    • Results in the aircraft deviating further from the equilibrium point
    • Aircraft has a lower longitudinal static stability

    #Part (b)

    Effect of positive aileron deflection:

    • Right/left aileron deflected down/up
    • Right wing generates more lift and thus more drag
    • Drag asymmetry causes aircraft to yaw right while aircraft is rolling left

    To achieve coordinated turn:

    • Apply positive rudder (deflection to the left)
    • Positive rudder generates negative yawing moment
    • Yaw moment causes aircraft to yaw left, in the direction of the roll

    #Question 2

    #Part (a)

    State and explain two advantages of a swept-forward wing.

    Improved maneuverability:

    • Sweptback wings tend to increase directional and lateral stability
    • Swept-forward wing therefore has lower directional and lateral stability
    • An aircraft with swept-forward wing will have less tendency to return to
      equilibrium without pilot input (deviate from equilibrium when disturbed)
    • Less stable aircraft is more maneuverable as pilot does not have to fight
      the aircraft as much when executing maneuvers since the aircraft has a
      lower tendency to “correct” the maneuver and return to equilibrium

    Improved stall characteristics:

    • At high α, flow over a swept-forward wing tends to flow towards wing root
    • Reduces likelihood of wingtip stall due to flow separation at the wingtip
    • Ensure control authority of the outboard ailerons

    For a sweptback wing, air tends to flow towards the wingtip. At high α, this will result
    in the wingtips stalling first, with the stall progressing inwards towards the wing root.
    As such, outboard ailerons (located nearer to wingtips) will lose its effectiveness as
    the stall progresses inwards to the wing root. This is undesirable as the outboard
    ailerons have a larger moment arm and thus, is able to generate a larger roll
    moment to correct the aircraft.

    #Part (b)

    For a conventional wing-tail aircraft, describe the expected sign of Cnδa​​​ for
    an aircraft exhibiting significant adverse yaw. Provide a detailed explanation.

    Adverse yaw:

    • Yawing moment in the direction opposite to the turn
    • Initial aileron deflection creates differential lift-induced drag
    • If aircraft is banking to the left, right aileron down, left aileron up
    • Right wing experiences more drag, causing aircraft to yaw to the right
    • Therefore, positive aileron deflection results in a positive yawing moment

    Total yawing moment is given by,

    Cn​=Cnβ​β+Cnδa​​​δa​+Cnδr​​​δr​

    Yawing moment due to aileron deflection is denoted by Cnδa​​​δa​.
    For a positive aileron deflection +δa​ to result in a positive yaw,
    the coefficient Cnδa​​​ must therefore be a positive value.

    #Part (c)

    #Part (i)

    Explain whether the 3-degree rudder deflection is aiding or
    impeding aircraft’s ability to maintain the sideslip approach.

    • Crosswind from the left results in a sideslip to the left
    • Aircraft will tend to yaw to the left to face the wind direction
    • +3° rudder deflection will generate a yawing moment to the left
    • Therefore, the rudder’s position is impeding the sideslip approach

    #Part (i)

    Flight speed of aircraft,

    V∞​=190 km/h=52.778 m/s

    Dynamic pressure,

    q=21​ρV∞​2=21​(1.225)(52.778)2=1706.1 Pa

    Sideslip angle,

    β=−tan−119020​=−6.01°

    Note that sideslip angle is negative as a negative
    yawing moment is required to correct the sideslip.

    Single engine failure during flight,

    0=−0.0032β+0.00036δr​−0.0024δa​+qSbLE​​ (1)

    0=0.0028β−0.0027δr​+0.00031δa​+qSbNE​​ (2)

    0=−0.019β+0.004δr​+qSWsinϕ​ (3)

    Required bank angle from (3),

    0=−0.019(−6.01°)+0.004(3°)+1706.1(19)9.81(5000)sinϕ​

    ϕ=−4.7838°

    Negative bank angle denotes a roll to the left.

    Aileron deflection from (1),

    0=−0.0032(−6.01°)+0.00036(3°)−0.0024δa​+0

    δa​=8.4633°

    Moment due to asymmetric thrust from (2),

    0=0.0028(−6.01°)−0.0027(3°)+0.00031(8.4633°)+1706.1(19)(12)NE​​

    NE​=8676.2 Nm

    Positive moment denotes a yaw moment to the right.
    Thus, we shall take clockwise moments as positive.

    NE​=TL​rL​+TR​rR​

    8676.2=3TL​−3TR​ (4)

    where TL​≡ thrust of left engine,
    and     TR​≡ thrust of right engine

    Total thrust force of both engines,

    7240=TL​+TR​

    TL​=7240−TR​ (5)

    Substituting (5) into (4),

    8676.2=3(7240−TR​)−3TR​

    TR​=2174.0 N

    TL​=5066.0 N

    #Part (c)

    Yaw rate and yaw angle feedbacks,

    (Δδr​)feedback​=k2​Δψ˙​+k1​Δψ

    Equation for pure yawing oscillation,

    Δψ¨​−Nr​Δψ˙​+Nβ​Δψ=Nδr​​Δδr​+Nδr​​(Δδr​)feedback​

    Δψ¨​−Nr​Δψ˙​+Nβ​ψ=Nδr​​Δδr​+k2​Nδr​​Δψ˙​+k1​Nδr​​Δψ

    Δψ¨​−(Nr​+k2​Nδr​​)Δψ˙​+(Nβ​−k1​Nδr​​)Δψ=Nδr​​Δδr​

    Characteristic equation,

    0=s2+(2ζωn​)s+ωn​2

    0=s2−(Nr​+k2​Nδr​​)s+(Nβ​−k1​Nδr​​)

    Natural frequency,

    ωn​=Nβ​−k1​Nδr​​​

    Damping ratio,

    ζ=2Nβ​−k1​Nδr​​​−(Nr​+k2​Nδr​​)​

    Let k1​=1 and k2​=1 to obtain expressions for the original values.

    ωn,1​=Nβ​−Nδr​​​

    ζ1​=2Nβ​−Nδr​​​−(Nr​+Nδr​​)​

    To double the natural frequency,

    2ωn,1​=Nβ​−k1​Nδr​​​

    k1​Nδr​​=Nβ​−4ωn,1​2

    k1​Nδr​​=Nβ​−4(Nβ​−Nδr​​)

    k1​Nδr​​=−3Nβ​+4Nδr​​

    3Nβ​=(4−k1​)Nδr​​

    k1​=4−Nδr​​3Nβ​​

    To double the damping ratio,

    2ζ1​=2Nβ​−k1​Nδr​​​−(Nr​+k2​Nδr​​)​

    4ζ1​Nβ​−k1​Nδr​​​=−(Nr​+k2​Nδr​​)

    4[2Nβ​−Nδr​​​−(Nr​+Nδr​​)​]Nβ​−(Nδr​​4Nδr​​−3Nβ​​)Nδr​​​=−(Nr​+k2​Nδr​​)

    −4(Nβ​−Nδr​​)​4(Nr​+Nδr​​)4(Nβ​−Nδr​​)​​=−(Nr​+k2​Nδr​​)

    4(Nr​+Nδr​​)=Nr​+k2​Nδr​​

    3Nr​=(k2​−4)Nδr​​

    k2​=4+Nδr​​3Nr​​
